newsitem.title: USA: NRC head calls for continued monitoring of ComEd.
newsitem.headline: NRC head calls for continued monitoring of ComEd.

text.p: The head of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission said Friday the NRC must continue to monitor Unicom Corp's Commonwealth Edison Co to ensure it can safely operate all its nuclear stations while improving performance.
But NRC Chairwoman Shirley Jackson raised concern that the commission did not have the resources to be able to scrutinize the company closely indefinitely.
"How long do you continue in the mode of intensive inspection application?" Jackson said at a commission meeting.
"If one is just...limping along, it's a question of where there is a cutoff point, just because of the finiteness of our own resources," Jackson said.
But she told reporters after the meeting that the commission was not contemplating ordering the company to close any of its plants at the moment.
The commission met Friday to hear from top ComEd officials about steps the company had taken in response to a January letter from the NRC.

In that unprecedented letter, the commission had asked the company to explain why regulator should have confidence that ComEd can operate six nuclear stations at the same time while sustaining performance improvements at each site.
"The commission remains concerned by the cyclic nature of performance at several Commonwealth Edison nuclear stations," Jackson said at the beginning of the meeting.
ComEd officials outlined several steps they had already taken to improve operator training and assessment of their own operations.
"We will not restart LaSalle or Zion until we have addressed the underlying performance problems," ComEd Chairman James O'Connor told the commission.
LaSalle and Zion were put on the NRC's watch list of unsafe plants in January while ComEd's Dresden nuclear station has been on the watch list since 1992.
NRC staff said that operations at Dresden and the company's quad cities had been improving while operations at the Braidwood and Byron nuclear stations were good.
The company was focusing its most aggressive actions at its Zion and LaSalle plants, ComEd Executive Vice President Thomas Maiman said.

While NRC staff approved of the program that ComEd had put in place to improve its operations, they said they needed more time to be able to judge whether the company was actually achieving its goals.
"We have a relatively high confidence level that the programs are quite solid," said Joe Callan, NRC executive director of operations. "They have worked elsewhere."
However, he said that ComEd had to be watched closely because "the record of ComEd in implementing programs in the past has been fairly dismal."
O'Connor told reporters after the meeting that what was different now is that there was a whole new level of commitment to change the culture of the staff at each of its nuclear stations.

"The level of resources is significantly higher than it has ever been in the past," he said, referring to the company's decision to spend $1.028 billion on its nuclear operations in 1997, up 11 percent from last year.
"There's no covering anything up," he said, adding that the company had been unusually open about its problems and what it intended to do to fix them.

O'Connor said the company had no current plans to shut down any of its nuclear units. But he added that the company was constantly reviewing which plants would be competitive in a deregulated power market.
"We are always considering what assets would be economic in the long haul," O'Connor said.
ComEd last week announced that it would close its Zion facility much earlier than 2013, when its license is due to expire, and most likely before 2005.
